New details on how the $6.3 billion Binance hack likely occurred:

According to initial reports, hackers compromised a Binance engineer's laptop, gaining access to internal systems used to authorize withdrawals.

The attackers then:

1. Hijacked a Binance hot wallet using Ethereum's EIP-7702 mechanism 

2. Redirected wallet transactions to a malicious smart contract

3. Transferred billions in crypto attacker-controlled wallets

4. Spread the stolen funds across multiple wallets and converted some assets into ETH to avoid freezes

The attack unfolded across multiple blockchains, with most funds drained in ~20 minutes.

~$3 billion of these funds have now been frozen, and Binance says it will cover all unrecovered hacking losses.

The full investigation remains ongoing.

How important are rates compared to earnings? Strong earnings growth will generally win the day over a rise in the cost of capital, and on that basis this bull market has hung in there nicely despite rising yields. Much of the market’s long-term valuation (5-year CAPE ratio) can be explained by just a few macro factors: margins, credit spreads, and yields. Below I did three regressions (covering 1960-2019). One is of margins and spreads vs the 5-year “forward” CAPE (which uses n18m estimates since 1985 in an attempt to be less backward looking) and the other also includes the nominal 10-year yield, and the third one adds in the 10-year term premium. 🧵(2/2)

Per the DCF model, the market’s intrinsic value is the present value of future cashflows. With earnings growth very strong, a rising cost of capital may not reverse a bull market but it could slow it down. Market history is full of examples of earnings-driven bull markets being interrupted by a tightening in financial conditions. One example is the 1994 Greenspan rate cycle, and another is the period from late 2014 to early 2016 when energy spreads blew out. A 2022 “echo” scenario remains a plausible scenario into 2027. 🧵(1/2)

Earnings season is off to a good start with 122 companies reporting so far and 80% beating estimates by an average 560 bps. Trailing earnings are up 33% from a year ago and the n12m estimate is up 39%. The difference between the n12m estimate and trailing earnings is 19% and decelerating. That suggests that a peak in the second derivative is forming. Investors rarely pay up for peak earnings growth, and this in part explains why the P/E-multiple is down 16% from a year ago.  The other factor is of course the rising cost of capital.
